title: When should a water utility run its lake pump, and how much of the saving is the tariff?
lede: Pump scheduling on EPANET's Net3 (WNTR): running the lake pump 21 h from 01:00 cuts pumping energy 52 % at a flat tariff because it idles the booster pump; the time-of-use tariff adds 3 to 16 % of cost at a ratio of 3 or less, and hourly on/off schedules (21,806 simulated, plus a GA) add almost nothing beyond one window once tank drawdown is priced (simulated, assumed tariff shapes).
summary: WNTR simulates Net3 for three days with pump 10 (the lake source) on a repeating 24-hour schedule, scoring the last day on pump energy (Net3’s 75 % efficiency) and time-of-use cost under three assumed tariff shapes with the peak/off-peak ratio swept 1.5–10. Feasible schedules keep the tanks in range and the daily balance within 1 %; pressure and tank range never bind. At a flat tariff the best window (01:00, 21 h) uses 1,307 kWh a day against 2,728 as shipped, 52 % less, because Net3’s river supply is mostly gravity and the booster pump 335 only runs when tank 1 is low, so more lake pumping idles it: a saving that needs no tariff. Beyond that, knowing the tariff adds 3.3 % of shipped cost at ratio 1.5, 15.8 % at 3 and 95 % at 10 for a 16:00–21:00 peak, and 3.1/12.1/39.2 % for a daytime peak. An exhaustive search of all 21,806 schedules with at most two on-runs a day finds a second window worth 0–0.02 % of cost for 8 of 10 tariffs (9.5 % and 1.2 % for the other two); a genetic algorithm and a local search over all 2<sup>24</sup> hourly schedules beat that by up to 4 points, but most of it is tank drawdown within the 1 % tolerance, and priced it falls to about 0–1.3 points. A first version mis-simulated windows that cross midnight; corrected here. One network, assumed tariffs (none sourced), no demand charge, a 1 % mass-balance gap not traced.
